{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=failure+modes+of+instruction-following+in+AI+systems+when+human+objectives+are+contextually+inadequate&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7433399\", \"title\": [\"When Agentic AI Breaks Software Quality Assurance: Failure Modes, Reliability Risks, and Governance Strategies for Autonomous Testing Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is changing software quality assurance from a predominantly human-directed activity into an increasingly autonomous process in which AI systems can generate tests, execute programs, interpret failures, modify test suites, and iteratively refine their actions. While these capabilities promise substantial improvements in testing speed, coverage, and engineering productivity, they also introduce a distinct class of quality risks. An autonomous testing agent can produce a technically executable test that encodes an incorrect assumption, misinterpret a failure, optimize for coverage rather than meaningful defect detection, or repeatedly reinforce an erroneous testing strategy. This article examines these risks through an integrative review of research on large language models (LLMs), automated software testing, AI-assisted software engineering, and AI governance. The analysis identifies six interconnected failure modes: erroneous test generation, defective test oracles, autonomous error propagation, coverage-driven quality illusion, contextual and repository misunderstanding, and governance and accountability failure. The article argues that the central challenge is not simply whether AI can generate valid tests, but whether autonomous testing systems can maintain trustworthy quality judgments under uncertainty. Drawing on empirical evidence from recent studies of ChatGPT, LLM-based test generation, TestGen-LLM, and software-engineering agents, the article proposes a risk-based governance model built around bounded autonomy, independent verification, traceability, human checkpoints, continuous monitoring, and explicit escalation mechanisms. The findings suggest that enterprise adoption should treat agentic testing as a controlled socio-technical system rather than a replacement for software quality expertise.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7433399\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1302/3114-220957\", \"title\": [\"Inadequate Proximal Fixation Can Increase Failure Following Plate Fixation of Diaphyseal Humerus Fractures\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1302/3114-220957\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022, 1, 13]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1145/3847307\", \"title\": [\"When Too Many Cooks Spoil the Broth: Three Failure Modes of Multi-Agent LLM Reliability\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>\\n                    Multi-agent LLM systems are widely deployed under three implicit assumptions: that self-confidence calibration transfers to peer evaluation, that errors made by distinct instances are statistically independent, and that any sufficiently calibrated model is an equivalent verifier. We test all three across GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Llama-3.3-70B. Self-confidence and peer-resistance dissociate: Claude shows the strongest self-confidence signal yet accepts every deliberately-wrong peer output, the opposite of what unidimensional calibration predicts. Four independent GPT-4o instances agree on the same wrong answer\\n                    <jats:inline-formula content-type=\\\"math/tex\\\">\\n                      <jats:tex-math notation=\\\"LaTeX\\\" version=\\\"MathJax\\\">\\\\(56\\\\%\\\\)</jats:tex-math>\\n                    </jats:inline-formula>\\n                    of the time on obscure factual queries versus\\n                    <jats:inline-formula content-type=\\\"math/tex\\\">\\n                      <jats:tex-math notation=\\\"LaTeX\\\" version=\\\"MathJax\\\">\\\\(0.4\\\\%\\\\)</jats:tex-math>\\n                    </jats:inline-formula>\\n                    predicted under independence—a\\n                    <jats:inline-formula content-type=\\\"math/tex\\\">\\n                      <jats:tex-math notation=\\\"LaTeX\\\" version=\\\"MathJax\\\">\\\\(140\\\\times\\\\)</jats:tex-math>\\n                    </jats:inline-formula>\\n                    violation. A pre-registered cross-family replication (\\n                    <jats:inline-formula content-type=\\\"math/tex\\\">\\n                      <jats:tex-math notation=\\\"LaTeX\\\" version=\\\"MathJax\\\">\\\\(N=200\\\\)</jats:tex-math>\\n                    </jats:inline-formula>\\n                    , three architecturally distinct families) yields\\n                    <jats:inline-formula content-type=\\\"math/tex\\\">\\n                      <jats:tex-math notation=\\\"LaTeX\\\" version=\\\"MathJax\\\">\\\\(55\\\\%\\\\)</jats:tex-math>\\n                    </jats:inline-formula>\\n                    three-way agreement, statistically indistinguishable from the same-family baseline (one-sided binomial\\n                    <jats:inline-formula content-type=\\\"math/tex\\\">\\n                      <jats:tex-math notation=\\\"LaTeX\\\" version=\\\"MathJax\\\">\\\\(p=0.41\\\\)</jats:tex-math>\\n                    </jats:inline-formula>\\n                    ): family diversification does not reduce correlated hallucination. Verifier choice produces a 42-percentage-point spread in error propagation. We propose a three-phase framework treating self-confidence assessment, peer-resistance capability, and error correlation as orthogonal axes requiring distinct training signals, and identify query-inherent rarity, not shared training, as the dominant driver of correlated failure.\\n                  </jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1145/3847307\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 9, 17]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6572478\", \"title\": [\"Why AI Agents Fail: A Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Autonomous LLM-Based Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are no longer a research curiosity-they are being deployed in production environments across industries. Yet for all the progress in what these systems can do, comparatively little attention has been paid to how, and under what conditions, they break. This paper attempts to fill part of that gap. Drawing on over forty published works from 2020 through early 2025, I propose a four-dimensional taxonomy of LLM agent failure modes, organized around the core functional modules present in most agentic architectures: reasoning and planning, tool use and action execution, memory and context management, and multi-agent orchestration.
